claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element alloy with principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios.
The starting catalyst has a low platinum-group-metal loading.
A post-synthesis hydrogen reduction treatment is the proposed intervention.
The hydrogen reduction treatment is to be conducted at moderate temperature for a short duration.
Hydrogen reduction induces selective surface restructuring of the multi-element alloy catalyst.
The selective surface restructuring forms a platinum-group-metal-enriched surface layer.
The platinum-group-metal-enriched surface layer acts as a protective barrier.
Hydrogen reduction removes detrimental surface oxides.
Hydrogen reduction drives a thermodynamically favorable rearrangement of surface metals.
The oxide removal and metal rearrangement create a stable active interface.
The resulting active interface resists sintering under realistic exhaust conditions.
The resulting active interface resists catalytic deactivation under realistic exhaust conditions.
Hydrogen treatment will increase NOx conversion efficiency relative to the untreated catalyst.
Hydrogen treatment will increase CO conversion efficiency relative to the untreated catalyst.
Hydrogen treatment will reduce activity loss during thermal aging relative to the untreated catalyst.
The untreated catalyst progressively deactivates under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The proposed benefits are expected under low-to-moderate thermal loads typical of gasoline or hybrid-vehicle operation, including exposure to H2O and NO.
Effectiveness at much higher temperatures or under significantly different exhaust compositions is uncertain.
Preliminary insights support the proposed mechanism and initial improvements.
